Chapter 1: Why Cooking Feels So Hard for So Many
Tell me if this sounds familiar. It’s the end of a long day, and you’re standing in your kitchen, just staring at the fridge. You know you need to make dinner, but honestly? It feels like climbing a mountain. For some people, the kitchen is a cozy retreat—a place to get creative and unwind—but for so many of us, it can feel more like a battleground. Stress, guilt, confusion... all wrapped up in the simple question, “What’s for dinner?”
Maybe you’ve had days like this: you open the fridge and it’s full, but nothing seems to fit together. Your mind races through worries—what if it turns out badly, what if it takes forever, what if I just can’t pull it off tonight?
You’re not alone in feeling this way. In fact, there are countless people who find themselves facing a pile of ingredients, quietly wishing dinner could just magically appear. Imagine a young professional who’s just moved into a new place. The kitchen’s tiny, there’s barely enough counter space, and all they’ve got is a box of pasta and a jar of sauce. After a draining day, even boiling water feels like too much. Ordering takeout is so tempting, but then there’s the cost... and that nagging feeling of guilt.
And for others, cooking brings up old memories. Maybe your parent whipped up incredible meals and made it look so easy, and now every attempt feels like falling short. Or perhaps you didn’t grow up cooking at all, so now even the basics feel strange and intimidating. Suddenly, the kitchen becomes a place of question marks and uncertainty.
It’s easy to start believing that cooking is only for people who truly love it, or that you need fancy gadgets and endless patience. And let’s be honest—food media doesn’t make it easier. Everywhere you look, there are perfect meals, intricate recipes, and spotless kitchens. If you already dread cooking, these images can make you feel like you’ll never measure up.
But here’s something important to remember. Feeding yourself doesn’t have to be complicated—or stressful. So much of the pressure to cook “the right way” is something we put on ourselves. The myth that every meal has to be a masterpiece? That’s what keeps a lot of people from even starting.
Picture this: a college student, completely wiped out from classes and work, opens the fridge and finds a half-eaten rotisserie chicken, some salad greens, and a couple slices of bread. Instead of giving up, she throws the chicken on some bread, adds a handful of greens, and calls it dinner. It’s not fancy, but it’s good—and it gets the job done. In that moment, she realizes: cooking isn’t about perfection. It’s about making something that works, with what you’ve got.
So, the first step to breaking through the dread of cooking? Let go of the idea that it has to be your passion, or some kind of performance. Most of us just want to eat something decent, without spending hours in the kitchen or feeling overwhelmed. The real challenge isn’t the food—it’s that mental wall that whispers, “I can’t do this.” Once you start chipping away at that wall, the kitchen slowly stops feeling like the enemy. It becomes a tool—a way to survive, to find comfort, and maybe even to feel a little proud of what you can do.
